# Celiac disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Celiac disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/YS0ny2)

---

## Summary

Celiac disease, also referred to as celiac sprue or nontropical sprue, is a common condition characterized by a maladaptive <u>immune response</u> to <u>gluten</u>, a protein found in many grains (e.g., wheat). The disease often occurs in patients with other autoimmune illnesses, as both are associated with <u>HLA</u> variants (<u>human leukocyte antigens</u>, which encode immunoregulatory <u>proteins</u>) that cause pathologically increased <u>immune responses</u>. The underlying pathophysiology is believed to be a combination of <u>gluten intolerance</u>, which triggers an autoimmune reaction, and production of <u>autoantibodies</u> that target <u>tissue transglutaminase</u>, specifically within the <u>proximal</u> <u>small intestine</u>. Typical findings include changes in bowel habits and symptoms associated with <u>malabsorption</u> (e.g., fatigue, weight loss, <u>vitamin deficiencies</u>). Diagnostic tests include the detection of various <u>antibodies</u>. To confirm the diagnosis, an endoscopic <u>biopsy</u> from the <u>small intestine</u> is needed. Histopathological findings often include villous <u>atrophy</u> and crypt <u>hyperplasia</u>. A definitive diagnosis is necessary, as therapy involves a lifelong commitment to a <u>gluten</u>-free diet. If patients comply with this diet, the prognosis is generally very good and the increased risk of celiac-associated malignancies (e.g., intestinal <u>lymphoma</u>) is mitigated.

---

## Definitions

* Definition: autoimmune disorder characterized by an intestinal hypersensitivity to <u>gluten</u>, a grain protein [[1]](/library/pj0LYT)

* Synonyms: celiac sprue; <u>gluten</u>-sensitive enteropathy

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u>

* Age of onset

* The disease can occur at any age.

* Peak <u>incidence</u> is bimodal:

* At 8–12 months (or 2–3 months following the first exposure to <u>gluten</u> through diet containing wheat)

* Third to fourth decade of life

* <u>Prevalence</u>: in the US ∼ 1:150  [[2]](/library/ZGXZBz)

* Race: more common in individuals of northern European descent




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Genetic predisposition with association to <u>HLA</u> <u>antigens</u> [[3]](/library/xj0EcT)

* HLA-DQ2 in 90–95% of patients

* HLA-DQ8 in 5–10% of patients

* Consuming <u>gliadin</u> from grains such as wheat, rye, and barley leads to an autoimmune reaction within the small intestinal wall.

* Commonly associated with autoimmune diseases (see “Clinical features” below)

---

## Pathophysiology

Symptoms manifest when a genetically predisposed individual develops an immunological response to <u>gliadin</u>, an <u>alcohol</u>-soluble fraction of <u>gluten</u>.



* Consumption of food containing gluten → tissue transglutaminase is released ;   → modifies <u>gliadin</u> from <u>gluten</u> <u>proteins</u> → pathogenic <u>T cells</u> react to and are activated by modified <u>gliadin</u> → mediate chronic intestinal inflammation → <u>epithelial</u> damage resulting in villous <u>atrophy</u>, crypt <u>hyperplasia</u>, and loss of brush border → impaired resorption of <u>nutrients</u> in the <u>small intestine</u> (especially in the <u>distal</u> <u>duodenum</u> and <u>proximal</u> <u>jejunum</u>) → <u>malabsorption</u> symptoms




![Celiac disease etiopathogenesis](media/yab5ql67xs57hnv09ww772tn.jpg)

Celiac disease etiopathogenesis

---

## Clinical features

### Gastrointestinal symptoms




* Chronic or recurring <u>diarrhea</u>

* <u>Steatorrhea</u>

* Flatulence, abdominal <u>bloating</u>, and <u>pain</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>/<u>vomiting</u>

* Lack of appetite

* <u>Constipation</u> (rarely)





### Extraintestinal symptoms and associations




* <u>Malabsorption</u> symptoms: fatigue, weight loss, <u>vitamin deficiency</u>, <u>iron deficiency anemia</u>, <u>osteoporosis</u>, <u>hypocalcemia</u>

* In children: <u>failure to thrive</u>, <u>growth failure</u>, <u>delayed puberty</u>, <u>secondary hyperparathyroidism</u>

* Dermatologic associations: <u>dermatitis herpetiformis</u>

* Neuropsychiatric symptoms: peripheral neuropathies (numbness, burning and tingling of the hands and feet) , <u>headache</u>, <u>ataxia</u>, <u>depression</u>, irritability [[4]](/library/Dj01cT)

* Gynecological associations: reduced <u>fertility</u> or <u>infertility</u>

* Endocrine associations: <u>autoimmune thyroid disease</u>, <u>type 1 diabetes mellitus</u>

* Associated <u>chromosomal</u> syndromes: <u>Turner syndrome</u>, <u>Down syndrome</u>

* Other associated conditions

* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis</u>

* <u>Irritable bowel syndrome</u>

* <u>Inflammatory bowel disease</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Selective IgA deficiency</u>

* <u>Atrophic glossitis</u>





> [!NOTE]
> In both children and adults, mild or asymptomatic cases are more common than the classic presentation of the disease.

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[6]](/library/S-by9w)[[7]](/library/U-bb9w)




* Celiac disease is an underdiagnosed condition that requires a high index of suspicion.

* Diagnosis is based on <u>serology</u> (initial testing) and <u>EGD</u> with <u>duodenal biopsy</u> (confirmation).

* A <u>gluten</u>-free diet can cause negative test results.

* <u>HLA</u>-based testing and/or a <u>gluten challenge</u> are options for patients not consuming <u>gluten</u>.

* Common indications for testing include:

* Symptoms of <u>malabsorption</u> (e.g., <u>steatorrhea</u>)

* <u>First-degree relatives</u> with celiac disease  [[6]](/library/S-by9w)

* <u>Iron deficiency anemia</u> unresponsive to treatment  [[6]](/library/S-by9w)

* <u>Elevated liver enzymes</u> with no discernable cause

* <u>Type 1 diabetes mellitus</u>

* Signs of <u>osteoporosis</u> (e.g., repeated, unexplained <u>fractures</u>)

* Workup of other autoimmune disorders (e.g., thyroiditis, <u>hepatitis</u>)





![Approach to celiac disease](media/oxfl13qcgzj8i9po68irbo6i.jpg)

Approach to celiac disease




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[7]](/library/U-bb9w)




#### Routine studies




* <u>IgA</u> tissue transglutaminase antibody (<u>tTG</u> <u>IgA</u>): initial test, crucial part of celiac disease serology

* Widely available test with high <u>specificity</u> (≥ 96%) [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)

* Risk of <u>false negatives</u> (e.g., in <u>IgA</u> deficiency, <u>gluten</u>-free diet)

* Total <u>IgA</u>

* Indicated for all patients because of the high <u>prevalence</u> of <u>IgA</u> deficiency in patients with celiac disease (approx. 2–3%)  [[3]](/library/xj0EcT)

* If patients have low <u>IgA</u>, perform further <u>IgG</u>-based testing.





#### Additional studies




* Deamidated gliadin peptide

* <u>IgG</u>-based testing: indicated in <u>IgA</u> deficiency or discordant <u>biopsy</u> and <u>serology</u>

* <u>IgG</u>-<u>tissue transglutaminase</u> (<u>tTG</u> <u>IgG</u>)

* <u>IgG deamidated gliadin peptide</u> (DGP IgG)

* <u>IgA</u>-based testing: <u>IgA deamidated gliadin peptide</u> (DGP IgA)

* <u>HLA</u> testing: second-line testing after unclear initial evaluation

* Assesses for haplotypes <u>HLA-DQ2</u> and <u>HLA-DQ8</u>

* Indications include:

* Uncertain diagnosis (e.g., disparity between <u>serology</u> and <u>histopathology</u>)

* <u>Gluten</u>-free diet prior to diagnosis

* Patients with <u>Down syndrome</u>  [[3]](/library/xj0EcT)

* Anti-endomysial antibody (<u>EMA</u>): Potential second-line <u>confirmatory test</u> (high-<u>specificity</u>)  [[7]](/library/U-bb9w)





### Endoscopy [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[7]](/library/U-bb9w)




* <u>EGD</u> with <u>small intestine biopsy</u> (<u>confirmatory test</u>) [[8]](/library/g-bF9w)

* Indications: positive <u>serology</u> or high clinical suspicion despite negative <u>serology</u>

* At least five <u>duodenal</u> <u>biopsies</u> should be taken (with ≥ 1 from the <u>duodenal bulb</u>).  [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[9]](/library/qaXCl9)

* Histological findings: typically ranked by severity according to the Marsh classification ;   [[10]](/library/HaXKN9)

* Intraepithelial <u>lymphocytic</u> infiltration

* Crypt <u>hyperplasia</u>

* Villous <u>atrophy</u>

* <u>Video capsule endoscopy</u>: if <u>EGD</u> is declined or as follow-up if symptoms persist despite treatment  [[11]](/library/h-bcCw)





> [!TIP]
> <u>False-negative</u> <u>serology</u> and <u>histopathology</u> results are possible if patients are already adhering to a <u>gluten</u>-free diet.

### Diagnosis without endoscopy [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[7]](/library/U-bb9w)




* Adults: diagnosis without <u>biopsy</u> not recommended.

* Children: consider diagnosis without <u>biopsy</u> in case of high <u>titers</u> of <u>tTG-IgA</u> and positive <u>EMA</u> (controversial)  [[12]](/library/ugXpCx)[[13]](/library/RaWl4P0)





### Further evaluation




* Gluten challenge: may be indicated if patients are already adhering to a <u>gluten</u>-free diet  [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)

* Systematic reintroduction of <u>gluten</u> into a patient's diet prior to (repeated) serologic and endoscopic testing

* 3 g <u>gluten</u> per day for up to eight weeks OR until the patient develops characteristic symptoms

* <u>Nutrient</u> deficiency screening (individualize): indicated in confirmed celiac disease [[14]](/library/e-bxww)[[15]](/library/T-b69w)

* <u>Ferritin</u>, <u>iron</u> (see “<u>Diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia</u>”)

* <u>Zinc</u>, <u>calcium</u>

* <u>Vitamin B12</u> and B6, <u>folate</u>

* <u>Fat-soluble vitamins</u>, especially <u>vitamin D</u>

* Associated autoimmune disorders: Consider further testing if there are symptoms for thyroiditis, <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u>, and/or <u>diabetes</u>.

* Tests for <u>malabsorption</u>: not routinely indicated (low <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>) 

* <u>D-xylose absorption test</u>: low urine <u>d-xylose</u> levels (The passive absorption of <u>d-xylose</u> in the <u>proximal</u> <u>small intestine</u> is impaired by the <u>mucosal</u> defect and bacterial overgrowth.)

* Fat <u>malabsorption</u>: quantitative stool fat assays or qualitatively via fat stains (e.g., <u>Sudan III stain</u>)

* See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Malabsorption</u>” for further information.





### Follow-up




* Repeat <u>laboratory studies</u> after 3–6 months and 12 months, then annually [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[7]](/library/U-bb9w)

* <u>tTG-IgA</u> or <u>DGP</u> <u>antibodies</u>

* <u>Nutrient</u> levels if the patient had a deficiency at the time of diagnosis [[8]](/library/g-bF9w)

* Endoscopy: only if symptoms persist or return in patients adhering to a <u>gluten</u>-free diet  [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[6]](/library/S-by9w)[[8]](/library/g-bF9w)

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Tropical sprue</u>

* <u>Whipple disease</u>

* Other wheat-related diseases, e.g., nonceliac <u>gluten sensitivity</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Diet [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[16]](/library/rZXf19)




* Strict, lifelong <u>gluten</u>-free diet  

* Abstain from products containing wheat, rye, barley, or spelt.

* Symptoms usually improve quickly  [[16]](/library/rZXf19)

* Recommended foods: rice, <u>corn</u>, potatoes, soybeans, millet

* Patients with <u>secondary lactase deficiency</u>: Avoid milk products.





### Other




* <u>Iron</u> and <u>vitamin</u> supplementation, if there are deficiencies (e.g., <u>iron deficiency anemia</u>)  [[15]](/library/T-b69w)

* Consider <u>osteoporosis screening</u> in adult patients  [[8]](/library/g-bF9w)

* Refer patients to a dietitian and advise joining support groups.  [[5]](/library/ZaWZQP0)[[8]](/library/g-bF9w)





> [!TIP]
> Managing celiac disease mainly consists of maintaining a lifelong <u>gluten</u>-free diet.

---

## Complications

* See “Clinical features” in “<u>Malabsorption</u>.”

* <u>Secondary lactase deficiency</u>

* Moderately increased risk of malignancies

* Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (<u>EATL</u>)

* Origin: intraepithelial <u>T cells</u>

* Localization: often <u>proximal</u> <u>jejunum</u>

* Clinical presentation: initially often asymptomatic, but <u>B symptoms</u> and gastrointestinal symptoms may be present

* <u>Adenocarcinoma</u> of the <u>small bowel</u>

* <u>Esophageal cancer</u> [[17]](/library/YGXnBz)

* Refractory celiac disease (<u>RCD</u>): persistence and worsening of celiac symptoms despite strict adherence to <u>gluten</u>-free diet for 12 months

* The condition manifests with one of three possible courses

* Only partial improvement despite <u>gluten</u>-free diet

* Initial improvement followed by relapse despite maintaining <u>gluten</u>-free diet

* Nonresponsive celiac disease (no response to <u>gluten</u>-free diet)

* May lead to <u>ulcerative jejunitis</u>

* In severe cases, <u>total parenteral nutrition</u> and treatment with <u>steroids</u> or <u>immunosuppressants</u> may be necessary.




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prevention

* There is no proven measure to prevent celiac disease.

* With <u>infants</u>, introducing small amounts of wheat (into the supplementary diet) between 4–6 months of age does not increase the risk of developing celiac disease

---
